# Results — Study 706 (Diamond Bottom)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
diamond bottom (range broadens then narrows, after a decline) calls the turn: buy the
upside break** — encoded as a mechanical rule, the direct bullish mirror of
[study 466's diamond top](../../466-diamond-top/). Pivots are confirmed fractals (k = 5,
with a 5-bar confirmation lag); over the 6 most-recent alternating pivots we require a
broadening leg (swing amplitudes rising) then a narrowing leg (amplitudes falling) — a
diamond — formed after a decline; a **long** fires on the first close above the narrowing
apex, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we measure the forward
5/10/20/60-day return of the long. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last
complete calendar month; the partial July bars on the tape are dropped). SPY fingerprint
`88127c764cba`.*

| Field | Value |

| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-06-30 (**As-of 2026-06-30**, partial July dropped; **21.5** years) |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) —
> labelled total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid
> ETFs; this is a single-instrument pattern study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so
> survivorship affects only the drift baseline (which the random-entry control neutralizes).
> The trade is a **long**, so it automatically banks the market's upward drift; the random
> baseline is also long, on random days — the drift helps both sides identically, which is
> exactly why the signal-vs-zero number below is *not* the test that matters.

## The signal — diamond-bottom long vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* against zero is the **misleading** number here (unlike the diamond-top
study, where drift punished the short for free, here drift *flatters* the long for free);
the **Welch breakout-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = breakout − random (both
are long returns).

| horizon | n | breakout (long) | win% | one-sample *t* | random (long) | Δ (breakout−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 197 | +30.2 bps | 58% | +2.57 | +44.2 bps | **−13.9 bps** | +28.2 bps | −0.69 | 0.492 |
| 10-day | 196 | +49.9 bps | 60% | +2.49 | +14.3 bps | **+35.6 bps** | +47.9 bps | +1.16 | 0.247 |
| 20-day | 195 | +66.4 bps | 61% | +2.22 | +91.9 bps | **−25.5 bps** | +64.4 bps | −0.55 | 0.581 |
| 60-day | 194 | +243.1 bps | 66% | +4.11 | +209.8 bps | **+33.3 bps** | +241.1 bps | +0.44 | 0.657 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks "significant" at **every**
horizon (+2.22 to +4.11) — and that is exactly the trap: a **long-only** rule on an
upward-drifting basket clears *t* = 2 against zero almost automatically, whether or not the
pattern means anything. Once we race it against the honest baseline — a random long on the
same instrument, epoch and hold — the apparent edge **evaporates**: Δ flips sign across
horizons (−13.9 / +35.6 / −25.5 / +33.3 bps) and the Welch *t* **never exceeds |1.16|**
(best case 10-day, *p* = 0.247 — not even close to the desk's bar). The diamond bottom does
not call the turn; it just happens to be a long, and longs get paid by the market's own
upward tilt.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent edge over random, either way

| ticker | entries | breakout (long) | one-sample *t* | random (long) | Δ (breakout−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 32 | +32.5 bps | +0.46 | +70.9 bps | **−38.3 bps** |
| QQQ | 42 | +112.0 bps | +1.70 | +107.7 bps | **+4.4 bps** |
| IWM | 49 | +44.2 bps | +0.72 | +53.2 bps | **−8.9 bps** |
| DIA | 46 | +66.3 bps | +1.37 | +101.8 bps | **−35.6 bps** |
| GLD | 28 | +74.1 bps | +0.71 | +125.9 bps | **−51.8 bps** |

Every single name's diamond-bottom breakout is positive in isolation (because it's a long on
a rising tape) — and every one of them is at or below what a random long on that same tape
earns, except a negligible +4.4 bps on QQQ. There is no ticker where the breakout
meaningfully *beats* the drift baseline. The pattern rides the tide; it doesn't add to it.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the diamond, nothing changes

The decisive "does the shape matter?" test: keep the pivot **positions** and the price
**marginal**, but permute which price sits at which pivot, so the broaden-then-narrow
diamond becomes geometric nonsense. If price genuinely respected *the diamond*, the scramble
would collapse the result.

| test | observed breakout (long) 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-pivot diamond | +32.5 bps | **0.842** | 500 |

**84% of scrambled-geometry "diamonds" match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.842) — an even
more decisive rejection than the diamond-top study's *p* = 0.679. The broaden-then-narrow
shape carries no information whatsoever; random nonsense diamonds do just as well or better.
"The diamond forecasts a reversal" is busted, for the bottom exactly as for the top.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real reversal

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* diamond-bottom reversal (knob `edge`: the upside
break is followed by a real sustained rally), the same long rule behaves exactly as it must
— so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a dead detector. The null
(edge = 0) is checked over **20 seeds** at `n_days = 8000` (never a single stream).

| world | n | breakout (long) | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| null (edge = 0), **20 seeds** | ~54 avg | — | — | mean **+0.03** (sd 1.07), **\|t\| ≥ 2 in 0/20 seeds** |
| edge = 0.00 (single seed 706, no reversal) | 62 | −54.1 bps | 42% | −1.07 |
| edge = 0.60 (real planted reversal, seed 706) | 46 | +1339.2 bps | 59% | **+4.42** |

With no planted reversal the control sits safely inside noise (mean *t* ≈ 0.03 across 20
seeds, never once clearing |2|); a real planted post-break rally lights up cleanly at
*t* = +4.42 with a 59% win-rate. The detector is live — it banks a reversal when one is
genuinely there, and finds none on the real tape.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The diamond-bottom breakout does **not** forecast an advance beyond
  what a random long on the same tape already earns. The one-sample *t* against zero looks
  significant everywhere (+2.22 to +4.11) purely because it's a long on a rising basket; the
  honest Welch breakout-vs-random test never exceeds |*t*| = 1.16 (best case 10-day,
  *p* = 0.247), and the sign of the delta flips across horizons. No ticker shows a
  meaningful edge over its own random-long baseline.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge to scale once the market's own
  upward drift is subtracted out — the breakout's apparent profitability is just beta with a
  diamond drawn on top. Costs (1 bp one-way × 2 legs) shave a little more off an edge that
  was never really there.
- **"Does the diamond shape forecast a reversal?" — BUSTED.** The shuffled-pivot placebo
  leaves the result untouched (*p* = 0.842, even more decisive than the diamond-top
  study's 0.679): geometric-nonsense diamonds match or beat the real ones, so the specific
  broaden-then-narrow shape carries no forecasting information. The diamond bottom is a
  descriptive label for a volatile consolidation during a decline, not a turn signal —
  exactly the mirror-image failure of its bearish twin.
